title: Product Discovery
summary: Finding out what is worth building before committing to building it.
what: Discovery is the work of reducing uncertainty about a problem before you spend engineering time on a solution. It answers four questions: is the problem real, is it valuable, can we solve it, and should we.
why: The most expensive failure in product work is building the wrong thing well. Discovery is cheap relative to delivery — a week of interviews costs a fraction of a quarter of engineering — and it is the only reliable defence against that failure.
analogy: A survey before construction. Nobody argues that surveying is wasted time, because everybody has seen what happens when a foundation is poured on the wrong ground.
technical:
The four risks worth naming separately, because they need different evidence:
- **Value risk** — will anyone use it? Evidence: interviews, existing behaviour, willingness to pay.
- **Usability risk** — can they figure it out? Evidence: prototypes, usability tests.
- **Feasibility risk** — can we build it? Evidence: technical spikes, prototypes with real data.
- **Business viability risk** — should we? Evidence: unit economics, legal, support load.

**For AI features, feasibility risk moves to the front.** In conventional software, if you can specify it you can usually build it. With AI, whether a model can do the task at acceptable quality is genuinely uncertain until you test it, so the first discovery activity is often a quality spike against real examples rather than an interview.

Discovery is continuous, not a phase. Teams that treat it as a stage gate ("discovery done, now delivery") stop learning at exactly the point where they start getting real signal.
diagram:
FOUR RISKS, FOUR KINDS OF EVIDENCE

     VALUE        will anyone use it?
                  → interviews · existing behaviour · willingness to pay

     USABILITY    can they figure it out?
                  → prototypes · usability tests

     FEASIBILITY  can we build it?
                  → technical spikes · real-data prototypes

     VIABILITY    should we?
                  → unit economics · legal · support load

   ⚠ FOR AI FEATURES, FEASIBILITY MOVES TO THE FRONT

     conventional software
       if you can specify it, you can usually build it
       → validate VALUE first

     AI features
       whether the model can do it at acceptable quality
       is genuinely unknown until you test
       → run a QUALITY SPIKE on 20 real examples first

     Because a validated problem you cannot solve
     is still not a roadmap item.

   DISCOVERY IS CONTINUOUS, NOT A PHASE

     ✗  discovery ──gate──► delivery
        stops learning exactly when signal starts

     ✓  discovery ⇄ delivery
        running continuously, informing each other

example.caption: A discovery week for an AI feature
example.code:
REQUEST  "Add AI so support agents can answer policy questions faster."

DAY 1 — FRAME THE RISK
  Value        agents ask policy questions ~40x/day (ticket data)     LOW risk
  Usability    it is a search box; they already use one              LOW risk
  Feasibility  can a model answer from our policy docs correctly?    ← UNKNOWN
  Viability    ~$0.02/query x 40/day x 60 agents = ~$1,400/mo        acceptable

  The dominant risk is FEASIBILITY. Start there, not with interviews.

DAY 2-3 — QUALITY SPIKE
  Pull 20 real policy questions from ticket history.
  Build the crudest possible pipeline: chunk the PDFs, embed, retrieve, answer.
  Score by hand against what the agent actually answered.

  Result   14/20 correct and cited
            4/20 correct but no citation
            2/20 CONFIDENTLY WRONG   ← the finding that matters

DAY 4 — INTERVIEW AROUND THE FINDING
  Ask five agents: "what happens if it is confidently wrong?"

  "I'd trust it the first few times, then stop using it entirely."
  "If it cites the clause I can check in ten seconds. If not I have to
   look it up anyway, so it saved me nothing."

  → citations are not a nice-to-have. They are the FEATURE.

DAY 5 — DECIDE
  Build: retrieval with mandatory citation, abstain when unsupported.
  Do NOT build: a confident chat assistant.
  Success metric: not "answers given" but "answers accepted without
  the agent opening the source document".

COST  one week and no engineering commitment.
      The version we would have built on day 1 was the wrong one.

questions.a: Value (will anyone use it), usability (can they figure it out), feasibility (can we build it) and viability (should the business do it). Each needs different evidence.

questions.q: Why does feasibility come first for AI features?
questions.a: In conventional software, a specification you can write is usually one you can build. With AI, whether the model reaches acceptable quality is genuinely unknown until tested, so a quality spike beats an interview as the first move.

questions.q: What goes wrong when discovery is treated as a phase?
questions.a: The team stops learning at the moment real signal starts arriving. Discovery should run continuously alongside delivery, each informing the other.

interview.s30: Discovery is reducing uncertainty about a problem before committing engineering time. I frame it as four risks — value, usability, feasibility, viability — and start with whichever one dominates.
interview.s90: For AI features that sequencing changes, and it is the thing I have seen teams get wrong most often. In normal software, if you can specify it you can build it, so you validate value first. With AI, feasibility is the genuine unknown — you do not know whether the model can do the task at acceptable quality until you try it on real examples. So my first move is usually a two-day quality spike on twenty real cases rather than a round of interviews. On a support-assistant project that spike found that two of twenty answers were confidently wrong, and when we took that specific finding back to agents, they told us citations were not a nice-to-have but the entire feature. title: User Research
summary: Learning what people actually do, as distinct from what they say they do.
what: User research is the systematic gathering of evidence about users' behaviour, context and needs. It spans qualitative methods (interviews, observation) and quantitative ones (surveys, behavioural analytics).
why: Product decisions are made on a model of the user. That model is either built from evidence or from assumption, and assumption is reliably wrong in ways that are invisible until launch.
analogy: A doctor examining a patient rather than treating the symptom the patient names. What people report and what is actually happening are related but not the same.
technical:
The methods split by what they can tell you:

**Qualitative** answers *why*. Interviews, contextual inquiry, usability tests, diary studies. Small n, deep insight, not generalisable to proportions.

**Quantitative** answers *how many*. Surveys, analytics, A/B tests. Large n, tells you scale, cannot tell you cause.

Using one where you need the other is the most common error: a survey cannot tell you why a workflow is abandoned, and five interviews cannot tell you what fraction of users abandon it.

**Behavioural evidence outranks stated preference.** What someone did last week is far more predictive than what they say they would do next week. Where you can, look at logs before you ask.

For AI features specifically, research must cover **failure tolerance**: what happens when the system is wrong. That is not a question users volunteer, and it usually determines the design more than the success case does.
diagram:
TWO KINDS OF QUESTION, TWO KINDS OF METHOD

     QUALITATIVE — answers WHY
       interviews · contextual inquiry
       usability tests · diary studies
       small n · deep · NOT proportions

     QUANTITATIVE — answers HOW MANY
       surveys · analytics · A/B tests
       large n · scale · NOT causes

   ⚠ THE MOST COMMON ERROR IS USING ONE FOR THE OTHER

     "what % of users abandon this?"      → analytics, not interviews
     "why do they abandon it?"            → interviews, not a survey
     "would you use this feature?"        → ✗ meaningless either way

   THE HIERARCHY OF EVIDENCE

     strongest   what they DID           logs, behaviour
                 what they DO            observation
                 what they SAY they do   interviews
     weakest     what they SAY they WOULD do   surveys about the future

   ⚠ FOR AI FEATURES, ASK ABOUT FAILURE

     users will not volunteer this, and it usually determines
     the design more than the success case does:

       "what would you do if it gave you a wrong answer?"
       "how would you know it was wrong?"
       "how many wrong answers before you stopped trusting it?"

     answers to the third question are typically 2 or 3.

example.caption: The same question asked four ways, with four different answers
example.code:
QUESTION  Should we build an AI summary of long support threads?

SURVEY (n=400)
  "Would you find an AI thread summary useful?"
    78% yes
  → almost useless. Nobody says no to a hypothetical convenience.

INTERVIEWS (n=8)
  "Walk me through the last long thread you handled."
    6 of 8 scrolled to the bottom and read only the last 3 messages
    2 of 8 opened the original ticket and ignored the thread entirely
  → the real behaviour is TRIAGE, not reading

ANALYTICS
    median thread length in tickets escalated twice: 14 messages
    median time-on-thread before first reply: 47 seconds
  → 47 seconds is not enough to read 14 messages.
    They are already summarising — badly, by skipping.

OBSERVATION (4 sessions, screen shared)
    every agent opened the CUSTOMER's messages and skipped
    internal notes entirely
  → a summary of the whole thread would summarise mostly noise

WHAT WE SHIPPED
  Not "summarise this thread."
  "What has the customer asked for, and what have we promised?"
  — two fields, extracted from customer messages only.

  The survey would have led to a generic summary feature.
  The observation led to a useful one.

⚠ THE FAILURE QUESTION, ASKED SEPARATELY
  "If the promise field was wrong, what happens?"
    "I'd repeat a promise we can't keep. That's a complaint."
  → promises must link to the exact message they came from.
    Non-negotiable, and nobody mentioned it unprompted.

questions.q: When should you use qualitative versus quantitative research?
questions.a: Qualitative answers why and cannot give you proportions; quantitative answers how many and cannot give you causes. Using one for the other is the most common research error.

questions.q: Why is "would you use this feature?" a bad question?
questions.a: It asks about hypothetical future behaviour, which is the weakest form of evidence. Almost nobody declines a hypothetical convenience, so the answer carries no signal.

questions.q: What research question is specific to AI features?
questions.a: What happens when it is wrong — how users would notice, what the consequence is, and how many errors they tolerate before abandoning it. Users do not volunteer this and it usually drives the design.

interview.s30: User research is finding out what people actually do, which is reliably different from what they say they would do. The method has to match the question — qualitative for why, quantitative for how many.
interview.s90: On a thread-summary feature, a survey of four hundred people said 78% would find it useful, which is meaningless because almost nobody declines a hypothetical convenience. Eight interviews asking "walk me through the last long thread you handled" showed six of eight scrolled to the bottom and read only the last three messages. Analytics said median time on thread before first reply was 47 seconds against a median of fourteen messages — they were already summarising, badly, by skipping. And watching four sessions showed everyone opened the customer messages and ignored internal notes, so a summary of the whole thread would have summarised mostly noise. We shipped two extracted fields instead of a summary. The survey would have produced a generic feature nobody needed.
interview.technical: The hierarchy of evidence runs from what they did (logs) through what they do (observation) and what they say they do (interviews) down to what they say they would do (surveys about the future). Using a qualitative method to size a problem, or a quantitative one to explain it, is the most common error. For AI features add a question users never volunteer: what happens when it is wrong, how would you know, and how many errors before you stop trusting it — the answer to the last is usually two or three.
interview.pm: Every product decision assumes a model of the user. That model is built either from evidence or from assumption, and assumption is wrong in ways that are invisible until launch.

title: Customer Interviews
summary: Asking about the past, not the future — and shutting up long enough to hear the answer.
what: A customer interview is a structured conversation about what someone actually did, aimed at understanding their problem rather than testing your solution.
why: It is the highest-signal-per-hour research method available, and it is also the easiest to do badly — a leading interview produces confident, comfortable, entirely wrong conclusions.
analogy: A detective interviewing a witness. You ask what they saw, not whether they agree with your theory, because the moment you name the theory they start confirming it.
technical:
The rules that do most of the work:

**Ask about the past, never the future.** "Tell me about the last time you…" rather than "would you…". Past behaviour is fact; future behaviour is speculation.

**Ask for stories, not opinions.** "Walk me through what happened" produces detail; "what do you think about X" produces a position.

**Do not pitch.** The moment you describe your solution, the interview becomes a politeness test.

**Follow the emotion.** Frustration, workarounds and improvised spreadsheets are where the real problems are. When someone says "it's fine, I just…", the thing after "just" is the finding.

**Silence is a tool.** The second thing someone says after a pause is usually more honest than the first.

Five to eight interviews with a coherent segment surfaces most of the significant patterns. Beyond that you get diminishing returns until you change segment.

Record the exact words. Paraphrased findings lose the specifics that make them actionable, and the verbatim quote is what convinces a stakeholder six weeks later.

THE FIVE RULES

     1  ASK ABOUT THE PAST
          ✓ "tell me about the last time you…"
          ✗ "would you use…"

     2  ASK FOR STORIES, NOT OPINIONS
          ✓ "walk me through what happened"
          ✗ "what do you think about…"

     3  DO NOT PITCH
          the moment you describe your solution,
          the interview becomes a politeness test

     4  FOLLOW THE EMOTION
          frustration · workarounds · improvised spreadsheets
          ⚠ "it's fine, I just…"
                              └─ THE THING AFTER "JUST" IS THE FINDING

     5  USE SILENCE
          the second thing someone says after a pause
          is usually more honest than the first

   HOW MANY?

     1-2   anecdotes
     5-8   patterns emerge          ← the useful range
     9-15  diminishing returns
     15+   change SEGMENT, not sample size

   RECORD THE EXACT WORDS

     paraphrase   "users want faster search"      → unusable
     verbatim     "I gave up and asked Priya on
                   Slack, she always knows"       → a whole design

     the verbatim quote is also what convinces a
     stakeholder six weeks later

example.caption: The same interview, run badly and run well
example.code:
BADLY
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PM   We're thinking about an AI assistant that answers policy
     questions instantly. Would that be useful?
USER Oh, that sounds great, yeah.
PM   And would you use it daily?
USER Probably, yeah.
PM   Any concerns?
USER Not really. Sounds good.

  Elapsed: 4 minutes. Learned: nothing.
  The user was being polite. Every answer confirms the pitch
  because the pitch came first.


WELL
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PM   Tell me about the last time you needed to check a policy.
USER This morning actually. Refund window on a damaged item.
PM   Walk me through exactly what you did.
USER Searched the handbook. Got about forty results. Gave up
     after two, and asked Priya on Slack — she always knows.
PM   [silence]
USER ...she's on leave next week, actually. I'm slightly
     dreading it.                                    ← the real finding
PM   How long did the Slack answer take?
USER Six, seven minutes? But the customer was waiting.
PM   What did you tell the customer during those minutes?
USER I said I'd check and get back to them. Which usually
     means they call again.                          ← the real cost
PM   Has the handbook search ever given you the right answer?
USER Honestly? I don't think I've ever scrolled past result three.

  Elapsed: 9 minutes. Learned:
    · search exists and is trusted so little it is not used
    · the actual system is ONE PERSON, and she takes leave
    · the cost is not agent time — it is repeat customer contacts
    · relevance matters more than coverage (nobody scrolls)

  None of that was in the roadmap. All of it came from
  asking about this morning instead of about next quarter.

title: Problem Statements
summary: Writing down the problem in a form that does not smuggle in the solution.
what: A problem statement describes who has a problem, in what situation, what it costs them, and how you would know it was solved — without naming a solution.
why: Most feature requests are solutions in disguise. Converting them back into problems is what makes it possible to find a better solution, to prioritise honestly, and to know afterwards whether you succeeded.
analogy: "I need a ladder" versus "I cannot reach the shelf". The first forecloses every option; the second admits a step stool, a lower shelf, or moving the item.
technical:
A usable statement has four parts:
- **Who** — a specific segment, not "users".
- **When** — the triggering situation. Problems occur in contexts, not in general.
- **What it costs** — time, money, errors, escalations, abandonment. Quantified where possible.
- **How we would know** — the observable change that would mean it is solved.

The last part does most of the work. A problem you cannot state a success signal for is a problem you cannot tell whether you solved, which means it will be declared solved by whoever shipped something.

**Test for a smuggled solution**: if the statement contains a noun that is a feature ("search", "dashboard", "assistant"), rewrite it. "Agents cannot find policy answers" is a problem. "Agents need a better search" is a solution wearing a problem's clothes.

For AI features, add a fifth part: **what a wrong answer costs**. That number determines whether the feature can be autonomous or must keep a human in the loop, and it is far easier to agree on before building than after.

     "agents need a better search"       ← solution in disguise
     "agents cannot find policy answers
      and ask a colleague instead"       ← problem

     no success signal
       → you cannot tell whether you solved it
       → it will be declared solved by whoever shipped something

     ✗  "Users want AI summaries."

     ✓  "Support agents (WHO), handling threads escalated twice
         (WHEN), spend 47 seconds skimming 14 messages and still
         miss commitments made earlier, causing ~30 repeat
         contacts/week (COST). Solved when repeat contacts from

Explaining why an obviously better feature was not adopted.

title: Jobs To Be Done
summary: People hire a product to make progress in a situation — not because of who they are.
what: Jobs To Be Done frames a purchase or usage decision as hiring something to make progress in a specific circumstance. The unit of analysis is the situation, not the person.
why: It explains competition that demographics cannot. Your competitor is whatever the customer would otherwise hire — which is frequently a spreadsheet, a colleague, or doing nothing at all.
analogy: The milkshake study: people bought milkshakes at 7am not because they were "milkshake customers" but because they had a long dull commute and needed something that lasted and could be handled one-handed. The competitor was a banana, not another milkshake.
technical:
The structure: **when [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome]**.

What it gives you that personas do not:
- **Situational competition.** The alternatives are whatever else could be hired in that circumstance, which is usually not another product in your category.
- **The forces of progress.** Push (dissatisfaction with the current approach), pull (the appeal of the new), habit (inertia), and anxiety (fear of the new). A feature that increases pull but does nothing about anxiety often does not change behaviour at all.
- **Stable targets.** Jobs change far more slowly than technologies or demographics.

**For AI features, anxiety is usually the binding force.** The pull is obvious and the push is real, and adoption still fails because people do not trust the output. Reducing anxiety — citations, visible reasoning, easy verification, reversibility — is usually higher leverage than increasing capability.

The failure mode is writing jobs so abstract they stop being useful. "When I want to be productive" is not a job. The situation has to be specific enough to observe.

THE STRUCTURE

     WHEN [situation]
       I want to [motivation]
         so I can [expected outcome]

     "when a customer asks about an edge-case policy mid-call"

       competitors:  asking Priya on Slack
                     guessing
                     saying "I'll get back to you"
                     the handbook PDF

       NOT: another AI assistant

     toward the new              away from the new
     ────────────────           ──────────────────
     PUSH                        HABIT
       the current way hurts       the current way is known

     PULL                        ANXIETY

title: Personas
summary: A shared shorthand for who you are building for — useful when grounded, harmful when invented.
what: A persona is a condensed description of a user segment: their goals, context, constraints and level of expertise, built from research and used as a shared reference across a team.
why: Teams make hundreds of small decisions that assume a user. Personas make that assumption explicit and shared, so the assumption can be challenged rather than silently differing between the designer, the engineer and the PM.
analogy: A composite sketch. Useful for coordinating a search; dangerous if you forget it was assembled from descriptions rather than photographed.
technical:
A persona earns its place when it is **derived from research** and when it **changes decisions**. A persona that lists age, job title and a stock photo but never resolves an argument is decoration.

The parts that actually matter: what they are trying to accomplish, what constrains them (time, permissions, expertise, device), what they currently do instead, and what would make them abandon your product.

**The main risk is invention.** Personas assembled in a workshop from what the team imagines are worse than no personas, because they carry the authority of research without the substance.

**Jobs To Be Done is often the better tool** when the same person behaves differently in different situations — which is most of the time. Personas describe people; jobs describe circumstances, and circumstances predict behaviour better.

For AI products, the persona dimension that matters most is not demographic but **expertise and verification ability**: can this person tell whether the output is correct? A persona who can verify tolerates a much more capable, more autonomous system than one who cannot.

title: Journey Mapping
summary: Laying out the whole path a user takes, so you can see where it actually breaks.
what: A journey map lays out the sequence of steps a user takes toward a goal, with what they do, think and feel at each step, and where the process breaks down.
why: Teams optimise the step they own. The failure is usually two steps earlier or in a handoff nobody owns, and that only becomes visible when the whole path is drawn on one page.
analogy: A route map rather than a photograph of one junction. Traffic problems are almost never caused where the queue forms.
technical:
The columns that carry the weight: **stage**, **action**, **touchpoint** (which system or person), **thinking/feeling**, **pain**, and **opportunity**.

Two properties make a map useful rather than decorative:
- **It crosses system boundaries.** The valuable findings are in the seams — where the user leaves your product for email, a phone call, a colleague, or a spreadsheet.
- **It is built from observation.** A map drawn from what the team believes happens reproduces the team's blind spots at higher resolution.

**Service blueprints** extend the map below the line of visibility to show backstage processes and systems, which is where the cause of a front-stage pain usually lives.

For AI features, add a row for **trust**: at each step, does the user believe the output, and what are they doing to check it? Verification effort is invisible in a conventional map and often eliminates the entire time saving the feature was supposed to produce.

title: Opportunity Sizing
summary: Estimating what solving a problem is worth, before deciding whether to solve it.
what: Opportunity sizing estimates the value of solving a problem: how many people have it, how often, what it costs them now, and what fraction of that cost a solution could realistically remove.
why: Prioritisation without sizing is prioritisation by whoever argues most persuasively. A rough, explicit estimate beats a confident intuition, mainly because it can be checked and corrected.
analogy: Estimating a repair before authorising it. The estimate will be wrong; having one still prevents spending a fortune on the wrong thing.
technical:
The structure: **frequency × population × cost per occurrence × realistic capture rate**.

The last term is where most estimates go wrong. A solution rarely removes the whole cost. If handbook search takes seven minutes and your assistant answers in thirty seconds, the saving is not 6.5 minutes — it is 6.5 minutes minus verification time, times the fraction of questions the assistant can actually answer, times the fraction of agents who adopt it.

**State the assumptions as numbers, not adjectives.** "Significant time saving" cannot be checked; "40 questions/day × 6 min × 60 agents × 70% coverage × 60% adoption" can be argued with line by line, which is the point.

**Bound it, do not point-estimate it.** Give a pessimistic and optimistic figure. If the pessimistic case is still worth doing, the decision is easy. If the optimistic case is not, the decision is also easy. Most of the argument only matters in between.

For AI features add a term the estimate usually omits: **the cost of being wrong × error rate**. A feature that saves ₹4 lakh a year and generates twelve incorrect refund commitments may be net negative.

THE STRUCTURE

     FREQUENCY  ×  POPULATION  ×  COST/OCCURRENCE  ×  CAPTURE

   ⚠ CAPTURE IS WHERE ESTIMATES GO WRONG

     naive     7 min → 30 sec = 6.5 min saved
     real      6.5 min
               − verification time
               × coverage (what fraction it can answer)
               × adoption (what fraction of people use it)
               = the actual saving

     a 6.5-minute saving at 70% coverage and 60% adoption
     is 2.7 minutes, not 6.5

   STATE ASSUMPTIONS AS NUMBERS

     ✗ "significant time saving"        cannot be argued with
     ✓ "40/day × 6 min × 60 agents
        × 70% coverage × 60% adoption"  can be argued line by line
                                        ← that IS the point

   BOUND IT, DO NOT POINT-ESTIMATE IT

     pessimistic still worth doing   →  decision is easy
     optimistic not worth doing      →  decision is easy
     in between                      →  the only case worth arguing

   ⚠ THE AI TERM MOST ESTIMATES OMIT

     + (cost of being wrong × error rate × volume)

     a feature saving ₹4L/year that produces twelve incorrect
     refund commitments may be NET NEGATIVE

example.caption: A sizing you can argue with, bounded rather than point-estimated
example.code:
def size(*, per_day, people, minutes_saved, coverage, adoption,
         verify_minutes, cost_per_hour, working_days=250,
         error_rate=0.0, cost_per_error=0.0):
    """Every input is a number someone can dispute. That is the point."""
    occurrences = per_day * people * working_days * coverage * adoption
    net_minutes = max(0.0, minutes_saved - verify_minutes)
    gross = occurrences * net_minutes / 60 * cost_per_hour
    errors = occurrences * error_rate
    return {
        "occurrences_per_year": round(occurrences),
        "net_minutes_each": round(net_minutes, 1),
        "gross_value": round(gross),
        "errors_per_year": round(errors),
        "error_cost": round(errors * cost_per_error),
        "net_value": round(gross - errors * cost_per_error),
    }

BASE = dict(per_day=40, people=60, minutes_saved=6.5,
            cost_per_hour=450, cost_per_error=2500)

print("PESSIMISTIC")
print(size(**BASE, coverage=0.50, adoption=0.40,
           verify_minutes=2.0, error_rate=0.06))
# {'occurrences_per_year': 120000, 'net_minutes_each': 4.5,
#  'gross_value': 4050000, 'errors_per_year': 7200,
#  'error_cost': 18000000, 'net_value': -13950000}
#                                        ↑ NEGATIVE

print("OPTIMISTIC")
print(size(**BASE, coverage=0.75, adoption=0.70,
           verify_minutes=0.2, error_rate=0.01))
# {'occurrences_per_year': 315000, 'net_minutes_each': 6.3,
#  'gross_value': 14883750, 'errors_per_year': 3150,
#  'error_cost': 7875000, 'net_value': 7008750}

# ⚠ THE BOUNDS DISAGREE ON THE SIGN.
#   This is not a "how big is the prize" decision — it is a
#   "can we get the error rate down and verification cheap"
#   decision. That is a completely different piece of work,
#   and the sizing is what revealed it.
#
#   Sensitivity says error_rate dominates everything else:
for er in (0.06, 0.03, 0.01, 0.005):
    v = size(**BASE, coverage=0.75, adoption=0.70,
             verify_minutes=0.2, error_rate=er)["net_value"]
    print(f"  error_rate {er:>5.1%} → net {v:>12,}")
#   error_rate  6.0% → net  -32,391,250
#   error_rate  3.0% → net  -8,754,250
#   error_rate  1.0% → net    7,008,750
#   error_rate  0.5% → net   10,946,250
#
#   The whole business case is a single number: can we get
#   below ~1.5% confidently-wrong answers. Everything else
#   is noise. Now go measure THAT.

title: Prioritization
summary: Deciding what not to do, in a way you can defend six months later.
what: Prioritisation is ordering work by expected value against cost and risk. The output is a sequence, and the meaningful part of it is everything you have decided not to do yet.
why: Capacity is fixed and demand is not. Without an explicit method, order is set by whoever escalated most recently, which produces a roadmap nobody can explain and a team that never finishes anything important.
analogy: Triage in an emergency department. The method is not about being fair to arrivals; it is about the fact that treating in arrival order kills people.
technical:
Common frameworks, and what each is actually good for:

**RICE** (Reach × Impact × Confidence ÷ Effort) — good when you have enough data to estimate reach and impact honestly. The confidence term is what makes it usable, because it penalises speculative bets rather than pretending they are certain.

**Value vs Effort** — a two-by-two. Crude, fast, and adequate for most decisions. Its weakness is that it hides risk.

**Weighted scoring** — explicit criteria with weights. Best when stakeholders disagree about what matters, because it moves the argument to the weights, where it belongs.

**Cost of delay / WSJF** — what does waiting cost? Strong for time-sensitive work like compliance deadlines and seasonal opportunities.

**None of them decide for you.** Their value is making the inputs explicit so the argument is about estimates rather than volume. A framework that produces a number nobody believes has still done its job if it exposed that two people meant different things by "impact".

**For AI work, add confidence explicitly and weight it heavily.** Feasibility is genuinely uncertain, so a high-value item with unproven feasibility should sort below a lower-value certain one — or, better, be replaced on the roadmap by the spike that resolves the uncertainty.

def rice(name, reach, impact, confidence, effort_weeks):
    """reach: users/quarter · impact: 0.25-3 · confidence: 0-1"""
    return {"item": name,
            "score": round(reach * impact * confidence / effort_weeks),
            "confidence": confidence}

BACKLOG = [
    rice("policy assistant (full)",    reach=60,  impact=3.0,
         confidence=0.30,              effort_weeks=8),
    rice("policy assistant SPIKE",     reach=60,  impact=3.0,
         confidence=0.90,              effort_weeks=0.6),
    rice("rank handbook search",       reach=60,  impact=1.5,
         confidence=0.90,              effort_weeks=2),
    rice("thread commitment extract",  reach=60,  impact=2.0,
         confidence=0.50,              effort_weeks=4),
    rice("dark mode",                  reach=200, impact=0.25,
         confidence=1.00,              effort_weeks=1),
]

for r in sorted(BACKLOG, key=lambda r: -r["score"]):
    flag = "  ⚠ low confidence" if r["confidence"] < 0.5 else ""
    print(f'{r["score"]:>4}  {r["item"]:<28} c={r["confidence"]:.2f}{flag}')

#  270  policy assistant SPIKE        c=0.90
#   68  rank handbook search          c=0.90
#   50  dark mode                     c=1.00
#   45  policy assistant (full)       c=0.30  ⚠ low confidence
#   15  thread commitment extract     c=0.50  ⚠ low confidence

# ⚠ THE SPIKE OUTSCORES THE FEATURE BY 6x.
#   Same reach, same impact — but three days instead of eight
#   weeks, and it converts a 0.30 confidence into a real number.
#   That is almost always the right first move on AI work.
#
#   Note also that dark mode beats the full assistant, which
#   feels wrong and is arithmetically correct given a 0.30
#   confidence. The fix is not to overrule the score. It is to
#   run the spike and re-score honestly next week.

# ── THE ARTEFACT THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS ─────────────────────
NOT_DOING_YET = {
    "thread commitment extract":
        "blocked on the same feasibility question as the assistant. "
        "Re-score after the spike (week of 8 Sep).",
    "dark mode":
        "scores well on effort but reach is inflated — 200 is all "
        "users, not users who asked. Revisit if it recurs in support.",
}
# Six months from now, this dict is the only thing that will
# explain why the roadmap looked the way it did.

questions.q: What is a prioritisation framework actually for?
questions.a: Making inputs explicit so the argument is about estimates rather than about who escalated loudest. A score nobody believes still helped if it revealed two people meant different things by impact.

questions.q: Why weight confidence heavily for AI work?
questions.a: Feasibility is genuinely uncertain, so a high-value item with unproven feasibility should sort below a certain lower-value one — or be replaced by the spike that resolves the uncertainty.

interview.s30: Prioritisation is ordering work by expected value against cost and risk, and the output I care about most is the explicit record of what we decided not to do and why.
interview.s90: I use RICE, but the term I lean on hardest is confidence, and that matters disproportionately for AI work. A feature with huge potential impact and thirty percent confidence in feasibility should not outrank a smaller certain win — and when I score it honestly, it does not. What usually happens is that the three-day spike scores several times higher than the eight-week feature, because it has the same reach and impact at a fraction of the effort and it converts the uncertainty into a real number. So the roadmap item becomes the spike. I have had that produce a result that felt wrong — dark mode outranking our flagship AI feature — and the right response was not to overrule the score, it was to run the spike and re-score the next week with a confidence figure we believed.

title: Roadmap
summary: A communication artefact about intent and sequence — not a delivery contract.
what: A roadmap communicates what a team intends to work on, in what order, and why. It is a statement of current intent that changes as evidence arrives.
why: Everyone outside the team needs to plan around what you will do. A roadmap that is honest about confidence lets them plan appropriately; one that reads as a set of dated promises destroys credibility the first time reality intervenes.
analogy: A weather forecast rather than a train timetable. Nobody is angry when a ten-day forecast changes, because the format communicates its own uncertainty.
technical:
The formats, in increasing honesty:
- **Dated feature list** — reads as a contract, breaks, damages trust. Appropriate only for genuinely fixed commitments like compliance deadlines.
- **Now / Next / Later** — the common default. Communicates sequence without implying precision on dates.
- **Outcome-based** — organised by the problem being solved and the metric expected to move, with solutions listed as current hypotheses. The most honest and the hardest to sell to stakeholders who want dates.

**Confidence should be visible.** Now items are committed and scoped; Next items are directionally agreed; Later items are problems, not solutions. Marking that explicitly prevents a Later item from being quoted back as a promise.

**For AI work, put the uncertainty on the roadmap itself.** A roadmap that reads "Q3: AI policy assistant" hides the fact that feasibility is unproven. "Q3: prove we can answer policy questions at under 2% error — then build" is both more honest and easier to defend when the answer turns out to be no.

Changing a roadmap is not a failure. Changing it without saying why is.

title: Product Strategy
summary: A diagnosis, a choice about where to play, and the small set of things that follow from it.
what: Product strategy is a coherent explanation of which customers you serve, what problem you solve for them, why you are positioned to solve it, and — crucially — what you are therefore not doing.
why: Without one, prioritisation has no reference point and every quarter is decided by whoever argues best. Strategy is what makes it possible to say no to a good idea, which is the only kind of no that is hard.
analogy: A military campaign plan rather than a wish list of objectives. The plan's value is in what it declines to defend.
technical:
A usable strategy has three parts (Rumelt's kernel):
- **Diagnosis** — what is actually going on. Where the leverage is, what the constraint is. Most strategy documents skip this and are unusable as a result.
- **Guiding policy** — the approach chosen in response. Broad, but it rules things out.
- **Coherent actions** — a small set of mutually reinforcing moves.

The test: **does it rule anything out?** A strategy that permits every plausible action is a mission statement. "Be the leading platform for X" rules out nothing.

Common failures: **goals mistaken for strategy** ("grow revenue 40%" is a target, not a plan); **a list of initiatives** with no thesis connecting them; and **strategy that never reaches the backlog**, existing only in a deck.

**For AI products specifically**, the strategic question that matters is where the durable advantage sits. Model capability is not a moat — it is available to competitors on the same terms and improves for everyone simultaneously. Advantage sits in **proprietary data, workflow integration, distribution, and the evaluation infrastructure that lets you improve faster than competitors can.** A strategy premised on having a better model is a strategy with an expiry date.

NOT A STRATEGY
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  "We will be the leading AI-powered customer support platform,
   delivering best-in-class experiences through cutting-edge
   models and delighting customers at every touchpoint."

  Rules out: nothing. Every possible initiative is consistent
  with this. It cannot decline a single request.


A STRATEGY
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  DIAGNOSIS
    Our advantage is not model quality — competitors call the
    same APIs we do, and capability improves for all of us at
    the same time. What we have that they do not is six years
    of resolved tickets with outcome labels, and an installed
    position inside the agent console.
    The constraint is TRUST: agents abandon assistive features
    after two confidently wrong answers, and we have no
    infrastructure to measure that before shipping.

  GUIDING POLICY
    Compete on verified correctness inside the existing agent
    workflow, not on breadth of capability.

    1  Build the evaluation harness first — golden set from our

    2  Ship only features that can cite their source and decline.
    3  Stay inside the console. No standalone app.
    4  Convert the ticket archive into a labelled retrieval corpus.

    ✗ fine-tuning a base model         (capability is not our moat;

    ✗ a standalone assistant app       (abandons our distribution)
    ✗ expanding to sales enablement    (different data, no archive,

    Declining good ideas is the only hard part of strategy,
    and it is only possible once the diagnosis is written down.

title: PRDs & Requirements
summary: Writing down what must be true, at the level of detail the decision actually needs.
what: A product requirements document states the problem, who it is for, what the solution must do, what it explicitly will not do, and how success will be judged.
why: Shared understanding decays fast. Six weeks after a conversation, three people remember three different agreements, and the cost of that divergence is discovered at the end rather than the beginning.
analogy: A building's plans rather than a sketch on a napkin. The napkin was enough to agree there should be a house; it is not enough to pour concrete.
technical:
The sections that earn their place: **problem and evidence**, **users and situation**, **success metrics**, **requirements** (what must be true, not how to build it), **explicit non-goals**, **open questions with owners**, and **risks**.

**Non-goals do more work than requirements.** They prevent scope drift and, more importantly, surface disagreement early — the argument you have about a non-goal in week one is the argument you would otherwise have in week six with code already written.

**Requirements state outcomes, not implementations.** "The answer must cite the source clause" is a requirement. "Use a citation component with a tooltip" is a design decision that belongs to whoever is designing.

Length should track the cost of being wrong. A reversible change to an internal tool needs a paragraph. A change to how money moves needs considerably more.

**AI features need sections a conventional PRD does not have**: acceptable error rate and how it is measured, the abstention policy, what happens when the model is wrong, what data is sent where, and the evaluation set the feature will be judged against. Agreeing those before building is what prevents "is 92% good enough?" being argued for the first time during launch review.

example.code:
FEATURE  Cited policy answers in the agent console

REQUIREMENTS (outcomes, not implementations)
  R1  Every answer cites at least one source clause, linked.
  R2  When retrieval returns nothing above the relevance floor,
      the system says so rather than answering.
  R3  Answer appears within 3s at p95.
  R4  Agent can report a wrong answer in one click, and the
      report captures the full trace.

NON-GOALS  ← the section that prevents six weeks of drift
  N1  Not customer-facing. Agents only, this release.
  N2  Does not draft refund approvals. (Agents cannot approve
      above ₹5,000 anyway — drafting one creates a worse moment.)
  N3  No conversational follow-up. Single question, single answer.
  N4  Does not cover regional policy variants. Out of corpus.

  ⚠ N2 caused a 40-minute argument in review. That argument
    was going to happen regardless. Having it in week 1 cost
    40 minutes; having it in week 6 costs a sprint.

── THE AI SECTIONS ──────────────────────────────────────────

ACCEPTABLE ERROR RATE
  Confidently wrong (answered, cited, incorrect):  < 1.5%
  Measured on:   golden set of 220 questions drawn from resolved
                 tickets, stratified: 120 common, 60 edge, 40 not-
                 in-corpus (correct behaviour = abstain)
  Judged by:     two support leads, independently, disagreements
                 resolved by a third. Re-run before every release.

ABSTENTION POLICY
  Abstain when   top retrieval score < 0.62, OR the drafted answer
                 is not supported by the retrieved text (groundedness
                 check), OR the question matches a regional variant.
  Abstention target: 25-35%. Below 20% means it is overreaching;
                     above 45% means it is not useful.
  ⚠ We are explicitly buying a HIGHER abstention rate to get a
    lower confidently-wrong rate. That is the central trade of
    this feature and it is stated here so nobody relitigates it.

WHEN IT IS WRONG
  Agent reports → trace stored → weekly review by PM + support lead
  → confirmed errors are added to the golden set as regression cases.
  Two confirmed policy-commitment errors in a week = feature off.

DATA FLOW
  Question + retrieved chunks → Anthropic API. No customer PII in
  the corpus (policy documents only). Zero retention configured.
  Traces stored 30 days in our own infrastructure, PII-redacted.

OPEN QUESTIONS
  Q1  Who owns the golden set after launch?        → Priya, by 8 Sep
  Q2  Does 3s p95 hold at 60 concurrent agents?    → Eng spike, 5 Sep

title: Epics & User Stories
summary: Slicing work into pieces small enough to finish and meaningful enough to matter.
what: An epic is a large body of work delivering a coherent outcome. A user story is a small slice of it, written from the user's perspective: as [who], I want [what], so that [why].
why: Work that cannot be finished within an iteration cannot be validated, and unvalidated work accumulates risk silently. Slicing is how you convert a six-week bet into six one-week bets you can stop after any of them.
analogy: A tasting menu rather than one enormous dish. Each course is complete and you learn something after every one.
technical:
The **so that** clause is the part that matters and the part usually dropped. Without it a story is a task and the team cannot make a sensible trade-off when the implementation turns out harder than expected.

**Slice vertically, not horizontally.** "Build the retrieval layer" is a horizontal slice — it delivers nothing usable and cannot be validated. "Answer one category of policy question end to end" is vertical: thinner, but it produces something a user can react to.

**INVEST** is the useful checklist: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. Most story problems are a failure of *valuable* (it is a task, not an outcome) or *small* (it cannot finish in an iteration).

**Spikes are legitimate stories.** For AI work, "determine whether we can answer policy questions below 2% error" is a real, valuable, timeboxed piece of work whose output is knowledge rather than software. Hiding that work inside a feature story is how estimates go wrong.

Stories are a conversation prompt, not a specification. The card is small on purpose; the shared understanding is built by talking about it.

title: Acceptance Criteria
summary: The conditions that decide whether something is done — agreed before it is built.
what: Acceptance criteria are the specific, checkable conditions a piece of work must satisfy to be considered complete.
why: Without them, "done" is negotiated after the work, by whoever has more energy for the argument. With them, it is a checklist, and the disagreement happens at the cheap end.
analogy: The pass conditions on an exam, published before the exam. Nobody argues about marking when the criteria were known in advance.
technical:
The two common forms: a **checklist** of conditions, or **Given / When / Then** scenarios which make the context, action and expected outcome explicit and map cleanly onto automated tests.

Good criteria are **observable** (someone else could check them), **binary** (met or not), and **written before implementation** — criteria written afterwards describe what was built rather than what was needed.

They must cover the unhappy paths: empty states, errors, permissions, and what happens at the boundaries. Most defects live there, and most criteria only describe the happy path.

**For AI features, acceptance criteria have to be statistical rather than deterministic.** "Returns the correct answer" is not checkable for a non-deterministic system. The checkable form is: on the agreed evaluation set, the confidently-wrong rate is below X, the abstention rate is between Y and Z, and specific named regression cases behave correctly. That reframing is what makes an AI feature releasable at all — otherwise it is either blocked forever on perfection or waved through on impression.

TWO FORMS

     CHECKLIST          GIVEN / WHEN / THEN
       · condition        Given  [context]
       · condition        When   [action]
       · condition        Then   [expected outcome]
                          ← maps cleanly onto automated tests

   GOOD CRITERIA ARE

     OBSERVABLE   someone else could check them
     BINARY       met or not met, no interpretation
     PRIOR        written BEFORE implementation
                  ← criteria written after describe what was
                    BUILT, not what was NEEDED

     empty states · errors · permissions · boundaries
     most defects live there
     most criteria only describe the happy path

     ✗ "returns the correct answer"
       not checkable for a non-deterministic system
       → either blocked forever on perfection,
         or waved through on impression

     ✓ on golden set v3 (220 cases):
         confidently-wrong        < 1.5%
         abstention rate          25-35%
         p95 latency              < 3s
         regression cases R1-R7   all pass

       THIS is releasable. The reframing is what makes
       an AI feature shippable at all.

example.code:
CONVENTIONAL STORY
  "As an agent, I want to flag a wrong answer in one click."

  ✓ A flag control is visible on every answer.
  ✓ Clicking it records: answer text, retrieved chunks, question,
    agent id, timestamp — in a single trace record.
  ✓ Confirmation appears within 500ms.
  ✓ The flagged answer remains on screen (it is not hidden).
  ✓ UNHAPPY: if the trace write fails, the agent still sees
    confirmation and the record is queued for retry.
  ✓ UNHAPPY: flagging twice does not create two records.
  ✓ PERMISSIONS: any agent can flag; only leads can dismiss.


AI STORY — the reframing that makes it releasable
  "As an agent handling a refund question, I want a cited answer."

  ✗ NOT THIS
    "Returns the correct answer for refund policy questions."
    — unfalsifiable. Correct for which questions? Judged by whom?

  ✓ MEASURED ON GOLDEN SET v3 (220 cases, 120 common /
    60 edge / 40 not-in-corpus)

      confidently-wrong rate       < 1.5%      (currently 0.9%)
      abstention rate              25-35%      (currently 29%)
      abstains on all 40 not-in-corpus cases   (currently 40/40)
      every answer carries ≥1 clause citation  (100%)
      citation resolves to a real clause       (100%)
      p95 end-to-end latency       < 3s        at 60 concurrent
      regression set R1-R7 pass                (7/7)

  ✓ JUDGED BY  two support leads independently; disagreements
               resolved by a third. Re-run before every release.

  ✓ UNHAPPY:   retrieval returns nothing above floor
               → "not covered by the policy documents I have"
               → NOT a generated guess
  ✓ UNHAPPY:   model API unavailable
               → existing handbook search shown, error logged
               → NOT a spinner that never resolves

  ⚠ THE ABSTENTION BAND IS A TWO-SIDED CRITERION.
    Below 20% means it is overreaching and will be wrong more.
    Above 45% means it is not useful enough to adopt.
    Only stating the lower bound would have shipped a system
    that declines everything and passes.

questions.q: Why must acceptance criteria be written before implementation?
questions.a: Criteria written afterwards describe what was built rather than what was needed, and "done" ends up negotiated by whoever has more energy for the argument.

questions.q: How do acceptance criteria change for AI features?
questions.a: They become statistical: a confidently-wrong rate below a threshold on a named evaluation set, an abstention band, and specific regression cases — rather than an unfalsifiable claim of correctness.

questions.q: Why state abstention as a band rather than a maximum?
questions.a: Only bounding it from one side lets a degenerate system pass. A model that declines every question has a perfect error rate and no value.

interview.s30: Acceptance criteria are the checkable conditions for "done", agreed before the work. Without them, done gets negotiated afterwards by whoever has more energy for the argument.
interview.s90: For AI features they have to be statistical rather than deterministic, and that reframing is what makes the feature releasable at all. "Returns the correct answer" is not checkable for a non-deterministic system — it either blocks forever on perfection or gets waved through on impression. The checkable form is: on golden set v3, 220 cases, confidently-wrong below 1.5%, abstention between 25% and 35%, all forty out-of-corpus cases abstain, every answer carries a resolvable citation, p95 under three seconds at sixty concurrent, regression cases R1 to R7 pass. The abstention band being two-sided matters — if we had only set a lower bound on quality, a system that declines every question would have passed with a perfect error rate and no value.
interview.technical: Given/When/Then maps cleanly onto automated tests. Criteria must be observable, binary, and written before implementation — criteria written afterwards describe what was built rather than what was needed. Cover the unhappy paths, where most defects live: empty retrieval, model unavailable, permissions, duplicate submission.
interview.pm: It converts the "is this good enough to ship" conversation from a judgement call under launch pressure into a checklist agreed while nobody was under pressure.

title: Backlog Management
summary: Keeping an ordered, honest list — and deleting most of it.
what: The backlog is the ordered list of everything the team might do next. Managing it means keeping the top of it ready to work on, the rest roughly ordered, and the whole thing small enough that people read it.
why: A backlog that nobody reads is not a plan, it is a graveyard. Its practical purpose is to answer one question — what should we pick up next — and a list of six hundred items answers that question worse than a list of thirty.
analogy: A kitchen prep list, not an archive. What matters is that the next few things are ready to cook.
technical:
**Refinement** is the ongoing work of making the top of the backlog ready: clarifying, slicing, estimating, and removing items that no longer make sense. It is continuous, not a ceremony.

The **depth of detail should decrease down the list.** The next two iterations of work should be sliced and have acceptance criteria; anything six months out should be a problem statement at most. Detailing far-future items is waste, because most of them will never be built.

**Deleting is the underrated skill.** An item that has been in the backlog for a year and never risen has been implicitly declined many times. Keeping it pretends a decision is still open. Delete it, and record the reason where the reason is discoverable — a declined list is more useful than a stale backlog.

**Bugs compete with features**, in the same list, ordered by the same criteria. A separate bug backlog means bugs are ordered by a different, usually worse, process.

For AI systems, add a distinct input: **confirmed error cases from production**. Every flagged wrong answer that gets confirmed should become both a regression case in the golden set and, where it reveals a pattern, a backlog item. That loop is what makes an AI product improve rather than just accumulate complaints.

     next quarter          ████      shaped, roughly sized

     detailing far-future items is waste —
     most of them will never be built

     different — usually worse — process

     production flag  →  confirmed?  →  regression case in golden set

title: Sprint Planning
summary: Agreeing what the team will attempt next, and why that set makes sense together.
what: Sprint planning is the session where a team selects work for the next iteration, agrees what it is trying to achieve, and confirms the work is understood well enough to start.
why: A sprint without a stated goal is a batch of unrelated tickets, and a batch of unrelated tickets cannot be traded off when something takes longer than expected. The goal is what lets a team drop the right thing rather than the last thing.
analogy: A crew agreeing on the destination before deciding what to load. The cargo list is negotiable; arriving is not.
technical:
The inputs: a refined backlog, known capacity (accounting for leave, support duty and meetings), and the previous iteration's actual throughput.

The outputs that matter: a **sprint goal** in one sentence, the selected items, and — importantly — a shared understanding of what would be dropped first if the sprint gets tight.

**Capacity is not headcount × days.** Support rotations, interviews, incidents and code review consume a large and fairly predictable fraction. Teams that plan at full capacity miss every sprint and learn nothing from missing.

**Estimates are for shaping the conversation, not for forecasting.** The value of estimating is the discussion that reveals two engineers understood the story differently. A team that estimates silently in a spreadsheet has kept the cost and discarded the benefit.

**For AI work, plan spikes as first-class items with hard timeboxes.** Research expands to fill available time, and "we'll look into whether the model can do this" is unbounded unless you bound it. Three days, then a decision, is a plannable item; "investigate" is not.

questions.a: It makes mid-sprint trade-offs possible. Without one, a team under pressure drops the last item on the list rather than the least important one.

title: Review & Retrospective
summary: Two different meetings: one about the product, one about the way of working.
what: A sprint review inspects the increment with stakeholders and adapts the plan. A retrospective inspects how the team worked and changes one thing about it.
why: They are routinely merged, and the merge destroys both. Review without stakeholders is a demo to nobody; retrospective inside a review becomes a status update where nobody says anything uncomfortable.
analogy: A dress rehearsal with an audience versus the cast meeting afterwards. Both are necessary and they cannot be the same room.
technical:
**Review** is about the product. Show working software, not slides. The valuable output is what you learn from stakeholder reaction, which frequently changes the next sprint's plan — a review where the plan never changes is theatre.

**Retrospective** is about the process. The output is exactly one change with an owner. Retros that produce eight action items produce zero, because nothing has an owner and nothing is checked.

The failure modes: retros that surface the same issue every time without resolving it (the issue is real and outside the team's control — escalate it or stop listing it), and retros with no psychological safety, which produce polite noise.

**Start the retro by checking the previous action.** If last time's change was never done, that is the most important thing in the room, and skipping it teaches the team that retro outcomes do not matter.

For AI work, add a standing review item: **what did production tell us this sprint?** Flagged errors, drift in the abstention rate, latency changes, cost per query. That is evidence the team would otherwise only see when someone complains.

Deciding which debt is worth paying down.
Auditing why an AI system cannot upgrade its model.
avoid: Paying down debt in code nobody touches.
Framing remediation as tidiness rather than cost.
mistakes: Treating all messy code as debt worth fixing.

title: Technical Debt
summary: The accumulated cost of past shortcuts, paid as interest on every future change.
what: Technical debt is the extra effort future work carries because of earlier decisions — deliberate shortcuts, decisions that were right then and wrong now, or code written without the understanding that arrived later.
why: It is the mechanism by which a team that shipped quickly for a year becomes a team that cannot ship at all, and it is invisible on any roadmap unless someone makes it visible.
analogy: Actual debt. Borrowing is often correct — it buys time you need now. What kills you is borrowing without noticing the interest payments, until they consume the whole income.
technical:
Useful distinctions, because they need different responses:
- **Deliberate and prudent** — "we shipped the simple version to learn; we will revisit". Legitimate, and only stays legitimate if it is recorded.
- **Deliberate and reckless** — "we do not have time to design it". Rarely worth it.
- **Inadvertent** — the code is wrong because nobody knew better at the time. Not a moral failing; still costs the same.

**Debt is only worth paying down where it charges interest.** A messy module nobody touches costs nothing. A messy module in the path of every feature costs on every feature. The question is not "is this ugly" but "how often do we pay".

**Make it visible in the same currency as features.** "Refactor the ingestion layer" competes badly against a customer request. "Every feature touching ingestion costs an extra week; we have four such features planned" competes well and is the same statement.

**AI systems accumulate a distinctive form**: prompts scattered across the codebase with no versioning, evaluation sets that no longer reflect production traffic, no tracing so failures cannot be diagnosed, and models pinned to versions nobody dares change. The last is the sharpest — a system with no evaluation harness cannot safely upgrade its model, so it is frozen on whatever it launched with while the field moves.

THE PITCH THAT LOSES
  "We need a sprint to refactor the retrieval layer. The code
   is messy and it's hard to work with."

  Stakeholder hears: engineers want to tidy up.
  Loses to: any customer-visible feature.


THE SAME REQUEST, IN THE CURRENCY OF THE ROADMAP
  "Four of the next six roadmap items touch retrieval.

   Measured over the last five features that touched it:
     estimated   5, 3, 8, 5, 3   = 24 days
     actual      9, 7, 13, 8, 6  = 43 days
     interest paid                 19 days (79% over)

   Cause: chunking, embedding and query logic are entangled,
   so any change requires re-verifying all three, and there
   are no tests at that boundary.

   Cost to fix: 8 days.
   Expected saving across the four planned items: ~15 days.
   Breaks even during this quarter, not eventually."

  ⚠ Same work. Same sprint. Now it is a scheduling decision
    with numbers rather than an aesthetic preference.


── THE AI DEBT AUDIT ────────────────────────────────────────
  ✗ prompts live in 6 files, 2 of them duplicated and diverged
       → cannot tell which version produced a given output
       → INTEREST: every quality investigation starts with
         "which prompt actually ran?"

  ✗ golden set built at launch, 14 months ago
       → traffic has shifted to regional variants not in it
       → INTEREST: passing evaluation tells us nothing.
         We shipped a regression that the set could not catch.

  ✗ no tracing
       → INTEREST: a wrong answer cannot be diagnosed. Every
         report becomes an unresolvable "we'll look into it".

  ⚠ model pinned to a version 14 months old
       → we cannot upgrade because we have no way to verify
         the new one is not worse
       → INTEREST: compounding. The gap widens every release,
         and the longer we wait the larger and riskier the
         eventual jump becomes.

  PRIORITY ORDER  tracing → refresh golden set → consolidate
                  prompts → then upgrade the model

  ⚠ Note the model upgrade is LAST, not first. It is the
    thing everyone wants and the thing that is unsafe until
    the other three are done.

questions.q: Which technical debt is worth paying down?
questions.a: The debt that charges interest — code in the path of upcoming work. A messy module nobody touches costs nothing; the question is how often you pay, not how ugly it is.

questions.q: How do you make debt work compete with features?
questions.a: State it in the same currency: the measured overrun on past features that touched the area, the number of planned features that will touch it, and the break-even point.

questions.q: What is the sharpest form of AI technical debt?
questions.a: A model pinned to an old version because there is no evaluation harness to verify a replacement is not worse. It compounds — the gap widens every release and the eventual jump gets riskier.

title: Trade-offs
summary: Every product decision gives something up — the skill is naming what, and choosing on purpose.
what: A trade-off is a decision where improving one dimension worsens another. Product work is largely the practice of identifying which dimensions are in tension and choosing deliberately between them.
why: Decisions presented as pure wins usually hide their cost, and the hidden cost is discovered by someone else, later, as a surprise. Naming the trade converts an argument about who is right into a discussion about what to buy.
analogy: An engineering budget. Weight, strength and cost are in tension in every part; the answer is not "make it strong" but "how much weight will we spend for how much strength".
technical:
The recurring tensions: **speed vs quality**, **scope vs time**, **flexibility vs simplicity**, **personalisation vs privacy**, **automation vs control**, and **short-term revenue vs long-term trust**.

The technique that does most of the work is stating the trade as a **purchase**: "we are buying two weeks of schedule by accepting a manual step for the first month". A purchase can be evaluated, priced and reversed. "We'll cut some scope" cannot.

**Reversibility should change how much you deliberate.** A decision you can undo in a week deserves a quick call; one that shapes a data model deserves a week of thought. Treating both the same is a common and expensive mistake in both directions.

**AI has its own signature trade-offs**, and they are unusually sharp:
- **Accuracy vs coverage** — abstaining more reduces errors and reduces usefulness.
- **Autonomy vs oversight** — every human checkpoint reduces risk and reduces the time saved.
- **Capability vs cost and latency** — a larger model is better, slower and more expensive.
- **Personalisation vs data minimisation** — more context means better answers and more data held.

These are not solvable. They are chosen, and the choice should be written down where the next person can find it — because the next person will otherwise "fix" the abstention rate without knowing it was set deliberately.

THE RECURRING TENSIONS

     speed ←──────────→ quality
     scope ←──────────→ time
     flexibility ←────→ simplicity
     personalisation ←→ privacy
     automation ←─────→ control
     short-term revenue ←→ long-term trust

   ⚠ STATE THE TRADE AS A PURCHASE

     ✗ "we'll cut some scope"
       cannot be evaluated, priced or reversed

     ✓ "we are BUYING two weeks of schedule by ACCEPTING
        a manual step for the first month"
       can be evaluated, priced and reversed

     shapes a data model   → a week of thought

     treating both the same is expensive in BOTH directions

   ⚠ AI'S SIGNATURE TRADE-OFFS ARE UNUSUALLY SHARP

     ACCURACY  ←──────────→  COVERAGE

       fewer errors            more usefulness

     AUTONOMY  ←──────────→  OVERSIGHT
       more time saved         less risk

     CAPABILITY ←─────────→  COST + LATENCY

     PERSONALISATION ←────→  DATA MINIMISATION

DECISION  Abstention threshold for policy answers
DATE      2026-03-14      OWNER  PM + Support lead
STATUS    Accepted        REVISIT  after 6 weeks of production data

THE TENSION
  Raising the threshold          Lowering it
    fewer confidently-wrong        answers more questions
    answers more "not covered"     more confidently-wrong

  These move together. There is no setting that improves both.

MEASURED (golden set v3, 220 cases)
  threshold   answered   confidently-wrong   agent-useful
    0.50        86%           4.1%              86%
    0.62        71%           1.1%              71%    ← chosen
    0.70        58%           0.6%              58%
    0.80        41%           0.3%              41%

WHAT WE ARE BUYING
  We are buying a drop from 4.1% to 1.1% confidently-wrong
  by giving up 15 percentage points of coverage.

WHY THAT PURCHASE
  · 5 of 11 agents said two confidently-wrong answers would
    make them stop using it entirely. At 4.1% and 40 queries
    a day, every agent hits two wrong answers within a week.
  · A "not covered" costs 6 minutes (they ask a colleague —
    the status quo). A wrong policy answer can cost an
    incorrect refund commitment and a complaint.
  · Asymmetric costs → buy accuracy with coverage.

WHAT WE ARE NOT DOING, AND WHY
  · Not 0.70: below ~60% answered, the feature stops being
    worth opening. Support lead's judgement, and the reason
    we set a LOWER bound on coverage as well as an upper
    bound on error.

REVERSIBILITY
  High. One config value, no data migration. This decision
  deserved two hours of thought, not two weeks — and it gets
  revisited with production data rather than argued again.

⚠ IF YOU ARE READING THIS BECAUSE ABSTENTION SEEMS HIGH:
  it is high on purpose. Before lowering it, re-run the
  golden set and look at the confidently-wrong column.

questions.q: What does framing a trade-off as a purchase achieve?
questions.a: It makes the decision evaluable, priceable and reversible. "We are buying two weeks of schedule by accepting a manual step for a month" can be argued with; "we'll cut some scope" cannot.

questions.q: Why should reversibility change how long you deliberate?
questions.a: A decision you can undo in a week deserves a quick call; one that shapes a data model deserves real thought. Spending equal effort on both wastes time in one direction and risk in the other.

questions.q: Why must AI trade-offs be written down?
questions.a: Because they look like bugs. Someone inheriting a high abstention rate will "fix" it without knowing it was set deliberately to buy a fourfold reduction in confidently-wrong answers.

interview.s30: Every product decision gives something up. I try to state the trade as a purchase — what we are buying and what we are paying — because a purchase can be priced and reversed, while "we will cut some scope" cannot.
interview.s90: The AI-specific version of this is sharper than most people expect, because accuracy and coverage move against each other directly. On a policy-answer feature we measured the abstention threshold across four settings: at 0.50 it answered 86% of questions with 4.1% confidently wrong; at 0.62 it answered 71% with 1.1% wrong. We chose 0.62, and the reason is asymmetric cost — a "not covered" costs six minutes because they ask a colleague, which is exactly the status quo, whereas a wrong policy answer can cost an incorrect refund commitment. Five of eleven agents told us two wrong answers would make them abandon it, and at 4.1% every agent hits two within a week. The part I care about most is that we wrote it down with the measurements, because the next person to look at a 29% abstention rate will read it as a defect and quietly lower the threshold.

title: Product Metrics
summary: Measuring whether the product is working, without measuring the wrong thing confidently.
what: Product metrics are the quantities a team tracks to know whether the product is delivering value: acquisition, activation, engagement, retention, and outcome measures specific to the problem being solved.
why: Without them, product success is asserted. With the wrong ones, it is asserted more confidently — which is worse, because a number ends arguments that should still be running.
analogy: Instruments in a cockpit. The danger is not having no instruments; it is an altimeter that reads high.
technical:
The distinctions worth holding:
- **Output vs outcome.** Features shipped, queries answered, sessions started — these are outputs. Whether the user's problem got smaller is the outcome. Teams drift toward outputs because they are easier to move.
- **Leading vs lagging.** Retention is lagging and definitive; activation rate is leading and actionable. You need both — one to steer, one to confirm.
- **Counter-metrics.** Every primary metric needs one that would catch the cheapest way to game it. Engagement paired with task completion time; answers-given paired with answers-corrected.

**Segment before concluding.** An overall average moving flat frequently hides one segment improving and another collapsing. The average is the least informative view of almost any metric.

**AI features need outcome and quality metrics tracked together**, because they trade against each other. Usage rising while corrections rise faster is not success. The set that actually describes an assistive feature: adoption, coverage (answered vs abstained), correction rate, downstream outcome, cost per interaction, and latency. Any one of those alone can be moved by making the others worse.

OUTPUT vs OUTCOME

     OUTPUT               OUTCOME
     features shipped     did the user's problem get smaller?
     queries answered
     sessions started     ← teams drift toward outputs
                            because they are easier to move

   LEADING vs LAGGING

     leading    activation rate      actionable, noisy
     lagging    retention            definitive, slow

     you need both: one to steer, one to confirm

   ⚠ EVERY PRIMARY METRIC NEEDS A COUNTER-METRIC

     primary                  counter (catches the cheap gaming)
     ────────                 ─────────────────────────────────
     engagement time     ⟷    task completion time
     answers given       ⟷    answers corrected
     tickets closed      ⟷    tickets reopened
     signups             ⟷    week-4 retention

   ⚠ SEGMENT BEFORE CONCLUDING

     overall           ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬  flat
       new users       ▲▲▲▲▲▲▲▲  +40%
       existing users  ▼▼▼▼▼▼▼▼  -22%

     the average is the LEAST informative view
     of almost any metric

   THE SET THAT DESCRIBES AN ASSISTIVE AI FEATURE

     adoption            who uses it
     coverage            answered vs abstained
     correction rate     how often it is wrong
     downstream outcome  did the real problem shrink
     cost per interaction
     latency

     ⚠ any ONE of these can be improved by making
       the others worse. Track them as a set.

def feature_health(week):
    m = {
        # ADOPTION
        "agents_using":        week.distinct_agents / week.total_agents,
        "queries_per_agent":   week.queries / max(week.distinct_agents, 1),

        # COVERAGE  (counter-metric to correction rate)
        "answered_rate":       week.answered / week.queries,
        "abstained_rate":      week.abstained / week.queries,

        # QUALITY  (counter-metric to coverage)
        "correction_rate":     week.flagged_confirmed / max(week.answered, 1),

        # OUTCOME — the only one that is not an output
        "repeat_contacts":     week.repeat_contacts,
        "verified_no_lookup":  week.answers_accepted_without_source_open
                               / max(week.answered, 1),

        # COST
        "cost_per_query":      week.spend / max(week.queries, 1),
        "p95_latency_ms":      week.p95_latency,
    }
    return {k: round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v
            for k, v in m.items()}

# WEEK 3 vs WEEK 9
#                          w3      w9
# agents_using           0.42    0.71   ▲ adoption up
# queries_per_agent      6.1     9.4    ▲
# answered_rate          0.71    0.59   ▼ ⚠
# abstained_rate         0.29    0.41   ▲ ⚠
# correction_rate        0.011   0.009  ▼ good
# repeat_contacts        26      19     ▼ THE OUTCOME IS MOVING
# verified_no_lookup     0.63    0.81   ▲ trust rising
# cost_per_query         ₹0.71   ₹0.68
# p95_latency_ms         2400    2380

# READING THIS SET, NOT ANY ONE NUMBER:
#   adoption up, outcome improving, corrections down.
#   BUT coverage fell 12 points — abstention is eating usefulness.
#   Correction rate improved partly BECAUSE coverage fell, which
#   is exactly why the two are tracked together.
#
#   Without answered_rate, the correction improvement reads as
#   a quality win. With it, it reads as a system that got more
#   cautious — which may or may not be what we want, and is now
#   a decision rather than an accident.

# ⚠ SEGMENT BEFORE CONCLUDING
# by tenure:
#   new agents (<3mo)     adoption 0.88   verified_no_lookup 0.91
#   senior agents         adoption 0.44   verified_no_lookup 0.62
#
#   Senior agents verify more and adopt less — they know enough
#   to doubt it. The overall 0.71 hid two different products.
