questions.q: What is a counter-metric and why does every primary need one?
questions.a: A metric that catches the cheapest way to game the primary — engagement paired with task completion time, answers given paired with answers corrected. Without it, improvement and gaming look identical.

questions.q: Why segment before concluding from a metric?
questions.a: A flat average routinely hides one segment improving and another collapsing. The average is the least informative view of almost any metric.

questions.q: Why must AI coverage and correction rate be tracked together?
questions.a: They trade against each other. A correction rate that falls because the system started abstaining more is not a quality improvement, and reading either number alone hides that.

interview.s30: Every primary metric needs a counter-metric that catches the cheapest way to game it, and every metric needs segmenting before you conclude anything from it.
interview.s90: On an assistive feature, our correction rate improved between week three and week nine — 1.1% to 0.9% — which reads as a quality win. Tracked alongside it, coverage had fallen twelve points, from 71% answered to 59%. The correction rate improved partly because the system had become more cautious, not because it had become more correct. Without the coverage metric next to it, that would have gone into a review as an improvement. The other thing that number hid was segment: new agents adopted at 88% and verified without lookup 91% of the time, while senior agents adopted at 44% — they knew enough to doubt it. The overall 71% described neither group.
interview.technical: Distinguish output from outcome — features shipped and queries answered are outputs, whether the user's problem got smaller is the outcome, and teams drift toward outputs because they move more easily. Pair leading with lagging: activation to steer, retention to confirm. For an assistive AI feature the honest set is adoption, coverage, correction rate, downstream outcome, cost per interaction and latency, because any one of those can be improved by worsening the others.

title: North-Star Metric
summary: One number that captures delivered value, with the guardrails that stop it being gamed.
what: A north-star metric is the single measure a team agrees best represents the value the product delivers to users, used to align decisions across functions.
why: Teams with several equally-weighted goals optimise whichever is easiest. One primary metric forces the trade-offs into the open — but only if it measures value received rather than activity performed.
analogy: A compass bearing, not a destination. It does not tell you which road to take; it tells you whether the road you took was the right direction.
technical:
A good north star has three properties: it **measures value the user receives** (not activity the product generated), it **moves when the product improves** (and not otherwise), and it is **something the team can actually influence** within a quarter.

The classic failures: **revenue** (lagging, and influenced by things the team does not control), **raw usage** (a support tool being used more may mean the underlying process got worse), and **anything with no counter-metric**.

**Guardrails are mandatory.** A north star without them selects for the cheapest way to move it. Pair it with two or three metrics that must not degrade — quality, cost, latency, trust.

The hard part is that the honest north star is usually harder to measure than the convenient one. "Questions resolved without escalation" requires joining systems; "queries answered" is in one log. Teams pick the convenient one and then spend a year confused about why it moves without anything improving.

**For an assistive AI product**, a north star built on volume is almost always wrong. Better: the share of interactions where the user got what they needed and did not have to verify it elsewhere — because that is the value, and it cannot be moved by answering more questions worse.

     2  moves when the product improves — AND NOT OTHERWISE

                    underlying process got WORSE
     no guardrails  selects for the cheapest way to move it

       NORTH STAR
            │
       ┌────┴────┬─────────┬──────────┐
     quality   cost     latency     trust
     must not degrade while the north star rises

example.caption: Choosing a north star, and the ones rejected
example.code:
PRODUCT  policy assistant inside the agent console

CANDIDATES CONSIDERED

  ✗ Queries answered per day
      Convenient — one log line. But it rises if the handbook
      gets worse, if agents ask the same thing twice because
      they did not trust the first answer, and if we lower the
      abstention threshold and answer more questions badly.
      Moves for three reasons, only one of which is good.

  ✗ Estimated time saved
      A model output, not a measurement. It is our assumptions
      multiplied by our traffic. It will always go up.

  ✗ Agent satisfaction score
      Lagging, noisy at our sample size, and it measures
      feelings about the whole console, not this feature.

  ✓ CHOSEN
      Share of policy questions resolved in-console without
      the agent opening the source document or asking a
      colleague.

      Why: it is value RECEIVED. It cannot be moved by
      answering more questions worse — a wrong answer sends
      them to the handbook, which removes it from the numerator.
      It cannot be moved by abstaining more either, because
      abstentions stay in the denominator.

      Current 0.44   ·   Target 0.65 by end of quarter

GUARDRAILS — must not degrade
  confidently-wrong rate      ≤ 1.5%      (now 0.9%)
  p95 latency                 ≤ 3.0s      (now 2.4s)
  cost per query              ≤ ₹1.00     (now ₹0.68)
  agent-reported trust        ≥ baseline  (quarterly survey)

⚠ WHAT THE GUARDRAILS PREVENT
  The cheapest way to raise the north star is to lower the
  abstention threshold — more answers, fewer colleague-asks.
  The confidently-wrong guardrail makes that path visible
  and blocks it. Without the guardrail, the north star and
  the gaming strategy are indistinguishable.

MEASUREMENT COST — stated honestly
  Requires joining console events, handbook opens and Slack
  activity. Three days of engineering, and a weekly job.
  We paid it. The convenient alternative would have cost
  a quarter of confused meetings.

questions.q: What makes a north-star metric good?
questions.a: It measures value the user received rather than activity the product generated, moves only when the product genuinely improves, and can be influenced by the team within a quarter.

questions.q: Why are guardrails mandatory?
questions.a: Without them the north star selects for the cheapest way to move it. Pairing it with quality, cost and latency limits makes improvement and gaming distinguishable.

questions.q: Why is volume a bad north star for an assistive AI product?
questions.a: Usage rises when the underlying process gets worse, when users re-ask because they did not trust the first answer, and when you answer more questions badly. It moves for several reasons, only one of which is good.

interview.s30: A north star is the one number that best represents value delivered to users, plus the guardrails that stop it being gamed. For assistive AI, volume metrics are almost always the wrong choice.
interview.s90: On a policy assistant we rejected "queries answered" precisely because it rises for three different reasons and only one of them is good — it goes up if the handbook gets worse, if agents re-ask because they did not trust the first answer, and if we lower the abstention threshold and answer more questions badly. What we chose instead was the share of policy questions resolved in-console without the agent opening the source document or asking a colleague. That cannot be gamed by answering more questions worse, because a wrong answer sends them to the handbook and removes itself from the numerator, and it cannot be gamed by abstaining more because abstentions stay in the denominator. It cost three days of engineering to join console events with handbook opens, which is the part teams usually skip — and skipping it buys you a quarter of meetings about why the convenient number went up while nothing got better.
